item.title: Kibidango: Momotaro's Millet Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Kibidango are small, soft, faintly sweet mochi dumplings dusted in powder, and in Okayama they carry a story: in the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, it is kibidango that the hero gives to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant to win them as companions on his journey to defeat the demons. Since the Kibi Plain west of Okayama is widely held to be the origin of that legend, the dumplings have become the prefecture’s defining souvenir.

item.title: Momiji Manju: Miyajima's Maple-Leaf Cakes — Guide
item.description: Momiji manju are little cakes baked in the shape of a maple leaf, a nod to the maples of Momijidani, and they are the definitive souvenir of Hiroshima. Created on Miyajima over a century ago, they are made from a light castella-style sponge batter poured into leaf-shaped moulds and filled traditionally with sweet red bean paste, though modern fillings run to custard, chocolate, matcha and cheese. On Miyajima you can watch them being made on rotating griddles and eat them still warm, which is a completely different experience from the boxed ones — and several shops sell them battered and deep-fried on a stick as age-momiji.

item.title: Nagasaki Castella Cake — Guide
item.description: Castella (kasutera) is Nagasaki’s most famous sweet, a moist, fine-grained sponge cake with a springy texture and a rich, honeyed sweetness, baked in a distinctive tall loaf with a brown top and bottom crust and a sticky layer of sugar crystals at the base. It was introduced to Nagasaki by Portuguese merchants in the sixteenth century — its name comes from ‘bread of Castile’ — and over 400 years Japanese bakers refined the simple recipe of eggs, flour, sugar and starch syrup into the beloved cake it is today.

item.title: Sata Andagi (Okinawan Doughnuts) — Guide
item.description: Sata andagi are Okinawa’s much-loved traditional deep-fried doughnuts, a simple, nostalgic sweet that’s an everyday treat across the islands. The name roughly means ‘deep-fried sugar’, and the recipe is straightforward — a batter of flour, sugar and egg is shaped into balls and deep-fried until crisp and golden on the outside while staying soft, fluffy and cake-like inside, often cracking open slightly at the top like a blooming flower. Slightly sweet and comforting rather than rich, they’re enjoyed by all ages and traditionally associated with celebrations and good fortune.

item.title: Shiroi Koibito Park — Guide
item.description: Shiroi Koibito Park, in western Sapporo, is a delightful chocolate-themed park created by Ishiya, the confectioner behind ‘Shiroi Koibito’ (‘White Lover’) — the famous white-chocolate-filled langue de chat cookies that are one of Hokkaido’s most iconic souvenirs. Designed like a whimsical European fantasy village, the park centres on a charming, storybook-style building complete with a clock tower, gardens and rose-filled grounds. Visitors can tour parts of the factory to watch the famous cookies being made, learn about the history of chocolate in a small museum, and take part in hands-on workshops to make their own giant Shiroi Koibito cookie or other sweets.

item.title: Hirosaki Apple Pie Trail: 50+ Shops to Taste — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki turns its apple heritage into a delicious tasting trail: over 50 bakeries, cafés and restaurants around the city each bake their own distinctive apple pie, from buttery lattice to French-style tarte. An official guide map ranks the pies, making an afternoon of tastings around the castle park easy and fun. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Shop hours vary (roughly daytime) Admission Pies ~¥300–500 each Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Year-round; autumn apple season peaks What to Try Over 50 distinct apple pies across the city.

item.title: Hokkaido Girls' Trip: Dairy Sweets, Otaru Romance & Lavender Fields
item.description: Hokkaido’s appeal for a girls' trip is different from Kyoto’s kimono-and-temple aesthetic or Tokyo’s shopping circuit — it operates on the level of landscape, dairy, and a slower pace that the southern islands rarely permit. The flower fields genuinely are as beautiful as the photographs suggest; the soft-serve ice cream made from milk that arrived from a farm that morning is a materially different object from anything sold in Tokyo; and the onsen ryokan experience in Noboribetsu or Jozankei has a depth of tradition that justifies being the trip’s centrepiece rather than an add-on.

item.title: Osaka Girls' Trip: Shopping, Sweets, Themed Cafes & Dotonbori Nights
item.description: Osaka is one of Japan’s most rewarding girls' trip destinations — the combination of fashion, food culture, entertainment, and city energy creates a trip that feels completely different from the temples-and-zen experience of Kyoto. The city’s directness and warmth translate perfectly to group travel: Osaka is a city that wants you to enjoy yourself, and it shows. 🛍️ Shopping Strategy Shinsaibashi — The Main Event Shinsaibashi-suji (心斎橋筋) is Osaka’s most complete shopping arcade — 600m covered, with brands at every price point.
